key_terms.meaning: N_A = k_c(C_A,b − C_A,s); mol/(m²·s), with bulk and surface concentrations C_A,b and C_A,s.
Flux per unit concentration driving force; N_A = k_c ΔC_A; units m/s.
Gas-side coefficient; N_A = k_G(p_A − p_A,i); usually mol/(m²·s·Pa).
Liquid-side coefficient; N_A = k_x(x_i − x_A); mol/(m²·s) per mole fraction.
1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x for dilute equilibrium y* = m x; based on gas mole fraction.
1/K_x = 1/k_x + 1/(m k_y); based on liquid mole fraction.
Sh = k_c L/D_AB; dimensionless mass transfer coefficient with length L and diffusivity D_AB.
Sc = μ/(ρD_AB) = ν/D_AB; momentum diffusivity divided by mass diffusivity.
Model with a stagnant film of thickness δ; k_c = D_AB/δ.
Eddies expose fresh surface for time t; k_c = 2√(D_AB/(πt)).
Surface elements renew at rate s; k_c = √(D_AB s).
Turbulent mixing contribution to mass flux; total flux uses D_AB + ε_M; units m²/s.
j_D = (k_c/u)Sc^(2/3) = f/2; links mass transfer to friction factor f.
Two stagnant films in series with equilibrium at the interface; resistances add.
A stage whose exiting liquid and vapor are in equilibrium; gives maximum separation.
E_MV = (y_n − y_n+1)/(y_n* − y_n+1); actual change over equilibrium change.

key_terms.term: Height of a transfer unit H_OG
key_terms.meaning: H_OG = G/(K_y a); packed height per transfer unit; G is molar gas flux.
N_OG = ∫ dy/(y − y*); dimensionless count of packed-column separation duty.
E = flux with reaction / flux without reaction; raises liquid-side mass transfer.
Ha = √(k D_AB)/k_L for first-order reaction; k is reaction rate constant.

takeaways: A convective mass transfer coefficient k_c turns a complex flow problem into a simple flux equation N_A = k_c ΔC_A.
Individual film coefficients add as resistances; the overall coefficient depends on which phase's driving force you choose.
Dimensionless correlations write Sh as a function of Re, Sc and geometry, so one measured system predicts another.
Film, penetration and surface-renewal theories give different physical pictures of the same k_c.
Momentum, heat and mass analogies let a friction factor or heat transfer coefficient estimate k_c.
At the interface the two phases are in equilibrium, so y_i = m x_i, and the two film resistances set the flux.
An ideal stage is an equilibrium stage; stage efficiency converts ideal stages into real trays.
Tray columns are counted in stages; packed columns are sized by H_OG multiplied by N_OG.
A reaction in the liquid film can raise flux by E, and Ha tells whether the reaction is slow or fast.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine coefficient definitions, the resistance-in-series derivation, one correlation or theory, and a staged or packed contactor calculation.

bank.q: Define the mass transfer coefficient k_c for convective mass transfer past a solid surface. Write the flux equation and state the units of each term.
outline: Definition as flux per unit concentration difference
N_A = k_c(C_A,b − C_A,s)
Units: N_A mol/(m²·s), C mol/m³, k_c m/s
Bulk and surface concentrations defined

bank.q: Derive the relation between individual and overall gas-phase mass transfer coefficients for dilute absorption, 1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x. Define m.
outline: Flux through gas film N_A = k_y(y − y_i)
Flux through liquid film N_A = k_x(x_i − x)
Interface equilibrium y_i = m x_i
Eliminate interface compositions to get 1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x
State assumptions: dilute, linear equilibrium, steady flux

bank.q: Compare film, penetration and surface-renewal theories of mass transfer. Give the k_c expression from each theory and state one limitation.
outline: Film: stagnant layer thickness δ, k_c = D/δ
Penetration: exposure time t, k_c = 2√(D/(πt))
Surface renewal: renewal rate s, k_c = √(Ds)
Compare predicted dependence on D
Limitations: film theory predicts k_c ∝ D; experiments often give D^0.5 to D^0.67

bank.q: Explain the two-resistance theory for interphase mass transfer. Why is the interface assumed to be in equilibrium?
outline: Two films in series, gas and liquid
Steady state: same flux through both films
Interface has no resistance, so equilibrium y_i = m x_i
Overall driving force split between films
Resistances add; one film may control

bank.q: A dilute gas is absorbed in a liquid. Given k_y, k_x and equilibrium slope m, calculate K_y and K_x. Find the percentage of total resistance in the gas film.
outline: Use 1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x
Use 1/K_x = 1/k_x + 1/(m k_y)
Gas-film resistance fraction = (1/k_y)/(1/K_y)
Keep units consistent for k_y and k_x
Check K_x = m K_y for the chosen definitions

bank.q: Air flows over a flat plate. Use a Sherwood-number correlation to estimate k_c from given Re, Sc, D_AB and plate length. State all assumptions.
outline: Choose correlation, e.g. Sh = 0.664 Re^0.5 Sc^0.33 for laminar flat plate
Compute Sh
k_c = Sh D_AB/L
Check laminar/turbulent range
State assumptions: constant properties, smooth plate, dilute species

bank.q: A tray column has a known equilibrium curve and operating line. Given the ideal number of stages and Murphree vapor efficiency E_MV, calculate the actual number of trays.
outline: Define E_MV = (y_n − y_n+1)/(y_n* − y_n+1)
Use stepwise construction with efficiency
Actual stages = ideal stages / efficiency only as an approximation
Explain why efficiency varies along column
Check final composition against specification

bank.q: For a packed absorber, given G, K_y a and the equilibrium relation, calculate H_OG, N_OG and packed height Z.
outline: H_OG = G/(K_y a)
N_OG = ∫ dy/(y − y*) between column limits
Use log mean driving force for linear equilibrium and dilute conditions
Z = H_OG N_OG
State units of G and K_y a

bank.q: A first-order reaction occurs in the liquid film. Given rate constant k, diffusivity D_AB and liquid-film coefficient k_L, calculate Ha and E. Decide whether the reaction is slow or fast.
outline: Ha = √(kD_AB)/k_L
For slow reaction Ha << 1, E ≈ 1
For fast reaction Ha >> 1, E ≈ Ha
Use E to correct flux N_A = E k_L C_A
State film-model assumptions

bank.q: Compare tray and packed contactors for gas absorption. Discuss stage efficiency, HTU, pressure drop, turndown and fouling.
outline: Tray: stagewise, efficiency concept, good turndown
Packed: continuous contact, H_OG and N_OG, low pressure drop per stage
Packed columns poor at very low liquid rates and prone to maldistribution
Trays handle solids and high liquid rates better
Choice depends on capacity, pressure drop and maintenance

bank.q: Analyse how gas velocity and liquid viscosity affect k_G, k_L and the overall resistance in a packed absorber.
outline: Higher gas velocity raises turbulence and k_G; also raises pressure drop
Higher liquid viscosity lowers D_AB and k_L
Resistance in series: 1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x
Identify controlling film from m and k values
Link to correlations: Sh depends on Re and Sc

bank.q: Evaluate film, penetration and surface-renewal theories against experimental Sherwood-number data. Which theory is most useful for design and why?
outline: Film theory gives simple k_c = D/δ but weak D dependence
Penetration and surface-renewal give k_c ∝ √D, closer to many experiments
Surface renewal has adjustable renewal rate s
Design correlations are empirical Sh = f(Re, Sc) rather than pure theory
Choose theory for physical insight; use correlations for sizing

bank.q: For a reactive absorption duty, choose a tray or packed contactor and size it. Include equilibrium, overall coefficient, reaction enhancement and stage or HTU calculation.
outline: Set equilibrium and operating lines
Choose contactor type from capacity and reaction needs
For trays: ideal stages and E_MV; for packing: H_OG and N_OG
Include enhancement factor E and Hatta number Ha
Check liquid holdup, pressure drop and temperature rise
State assumptions and safety margin

glossary.def: A coefficient that gives mass flux per unit concentration driving force across a fluid phase.
Mass transfer from a moving fluid to a surface or another fluid, helped by bulk flow and turbulence.
Transfer of a component from one phase to another across their interface, as in absorption or extraction.
A coefficient for one phase film, such as gas-film k_y or liquid-film k_x.
A coefficient based on the total driving force from bulk gas to bulk liquid, written K_y or K_x.
A constant relating gas partial pressure to liquid mole fraction at equilibrium, p_A = H x_A.
A plot of equilibrium vapor composition against liquid composition at fixed temperature and pressure.
A material-balance line relating vapor and liquid compositions in a stage or packed contactor.
A model with one gas film and one liquid film in series, with equilibrium at the interface.
A model that treats resistance as a stagnant film of fixed thickness δ, giving k_c = D/δ.
A model in which fluid elements contact the interface for a short time t, giving k_c ∝ √(D/t).
A model in which surface elements are replaced at a renewal rate s, giving k_c = √(Ds).
Turbulent mixing that increases transport beyond molecular diffusion, described by eddy diffusivity.
A dimensionless mass transfer coefficient, Sh = k_c L/D_AB.
A dimensionless ratio of momentum diffusivity to mass diffusivity, Sc = μ/(ρD_AB).
A dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous forces, Re = ρuL/μ, used in flow correlations.
An analogy linking mass transfer and friction through j_D = (k_c/u)Sc^(2/3) = f/2.
A hypothetical stage that leaves its exiting vapor and liquid in equilibrium.
The ratio of the composition change in a real stage to that in an ideal equilibrium stage.
The packed height needed for one transfer unit, H_OG = G/(K_y a).
A dimensionless measure of separation duty, N_OG = ∫ dy/(y − y*).
A continuous-contact column filled with packing that provides interfacial area for mass transfer.
A stagewise column with plates or trays on which vapor bubbles through liquid.
The factor by which a chemical reaction increases mass flux above physical absorption.
A dimensionless number comparing reaction rate to diffusion rate in the liquid film.
Gas absorption in which the dissolved gas reacts with a component in the liquid.
